links.note: 311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that yields eminence (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). 328 says that however great the gain that brings good, gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை). Adjacent chapters use the same concessive form to refuse the same trade, once for hurt and once for killing; Parimelazhagar narrows both, to yogic powers in 311 and to sacrifice in 328.

113 tells one to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை). 311 refuses wealth that would require hurting others (பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்யாமை). Both grant that the gain is real and still rule out the means, one in the householder's ethics and one in the renouncer's.

755, in the chapter on making wealth, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்) should be let go and not embraced. 311 makes not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless even at the cost of wealth. The condition that 311 states for the pure is repeated in the Book of Wealth as a rule for acquisition itself.

312 says that even when someone in hatred has done hurt (கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்), not hurting back is the stand of the stainless. 157 says that though others do what is improper to you, it is good to feel the pain and not do what is contrary to virtue (நோநொந்து அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று). The forbearance chapter states for the householder what 312 states as a renouncer's resolve; Parimelazhagar reads the pain in 157 as pity for the wrongdoer.

852, on hostility, says that even if someone does unbearable things intending division, not doing hurt in return out of hostility is the highest course (இகல்கருதி இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). 312 says not hurting in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the stand of the stainless. The same rule, in nearly the same words, is carried from personal purity into the politics of faction.

313 says that doing hurt, even to those who hated you though you did nothing to them (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), brings sorrow with no escape (உய்யா விழுமம்). 207 says people escape any enmity (உய்வர்) but the enmity of their own deeds follows and kills (வினைப்பகை வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்). The shared root உய் shows the reasoning: an enemy can be survived, one's own retaliation cannot.

314 defines punishing those who hurt you as doing them good so that they are ashamed (அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 987 asks what worth (சால்பு) has achieved if one does not do sweet things even to those who did harm (இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). Both open on the same words, இன்னாசெய்தார்; the Book of Virtue gives it as a method, the Book of Wealth as the test of character.

158 says to defeat those who did wrong out of arrogance by one's own worthiness (தம் தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as forbearance. 314 goes a step further: do them a kindness so that they feel shame. Both keep the vocabulary of contest (winning, punishing) while replacing retaliation, and 314 adds the active good that 158 leaves unstated.

152 says bearing an excess done to you is good and forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 314 ends on விடல்: do good and let it go. Parimelazhagar takes this விடல் as forgetting both the hurt and the good done in return, which would make 314 the fuller form of 152's advice; the Tamil itself says only 'do and leave'.

315 asks what understanding achieves (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own. 203 says the chief of all understanding (அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலை) is not doing harm even to those who hate you. Read together they define அறிவு by non-harm: 203 positively, 315 by denying that anything else called understanding is of use.

315 asks for another's pain to be guarded against like one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). 1015 says the world calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace and their own alike (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார்) the dwelling of shame. The same extension of a self-regarding feeling to others is made for pain in the Book of Virtue and for disgrace in the Book of Wealth.

120 says true trade for traders is caring for others' goods as their own (பிறவும் தமபோல் செயின்). 315 says understanding is useless unless another's pain is guarded like one's own (தந்நோய்போல்). The 'as one's own' measure is applied to goods in fair dealing and to suffering in non-harm.

316 says what one has perceived as painful (இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை) one must not come near doing to another. 250 gives a way to perceive it: when going against the weaker, think of yourself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). 316 states the rule from one's own experience of pain; 250 supplies the act of imagination for the moment one has the upper hand.

317 calls it the highest thing not to do ill of any degree, at any time, to anyone, where the ill arises from the mind (மனத்தானாம் மாணா). 282 says even thinking in the heart of stealing another's goods is wrong (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே). Both locate the fault in the mind before any act; Manakkudavar reads 317 as 'even with the mind', while Parimelazhagar takes it as ill done with intent.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 317 makes the highest thing the absence of any mind-born ill toward anyone (மனத்தானாம் மாணா செய்யாமை தலை), in a chapter whose first two verses speak of the மாசற்றார். 317 gives 34's general claim a specific content: the unstained mind is one that harbours no hurt.

316 gives the rule: what one has perceived as painful, do not do to another (துன்னாமை வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்). 318 turns it into a question: one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான்), why (என்கொலோ) does he hurt other lives? The second verse treats breaking the rule as something needing explanation; Parimelazhagar suggests delusion as the implied answer. (The edition's text of 318 has typos in its first line.)

209 says that if a person loves himself (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்) he should not come near evil deeds, however small. 318 asks why one who knows what hurts his own life does hurt to other lives. Both reason from self-regard, by different routes: 209 from the doer's own interest, 318 from the doer's own knowledge of pain.

319 says that if you do hurt to others in the forenoon, hurt comes to you in the afternoon of itself (தாமே வரும்). 204 says do not plot another's ruin, for virtue plots the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). Both make the return of harm automatic and close in time; 204 names அறம் as the agent where 319 leaves it as coming by itself.

208 says the ruin of those who do evil is like a shadow that never leaves and rests at the foot (நிழல் ... அடி உறைந்தற்று). 319 puts the same inevitability in time: forenoon and afternoon (முற்பகல், பிற்பகல்). One verse uses space and the other the day's two halves to say that consequence is attached to the deed; the day figure also fits a shadow lengthening after noon, though the text does not say so.

320 says all pains rest on those who caused pain, so those who want freedom from pain cause none (நோய்செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர்). 206 says one who does not want afflicting things to overpower him (நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான்) should not do evil to others. The two verses give the same prudential argument in the same vocabulary of நோய், one closing the renouncer's chapter on non-harm and one in the householder's chapter on fearing evil deeds.

320 says all pains fall on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 169 admits that the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright meet ruin, and says only that this is to be pondered (நினைக்கப் படும்). 169 concedes cases that 320's rule does not show on its face; Manakkudavar's reading of 320, that present pain comes from hurt done earlier, and Parimelazhagar's of 169, that such cases are to be examined for causes, are the way the commentators reconcile them.

331 calls lowest the paltry understanding that takes what does not last for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்). 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). The two verses are built on the same sentence frame; 331 applies the misperception to duration and 351 to reality, and 351 adds the consequence, rebirth.

349 says the moment attachment ends births are cut off, and otherwise impermanence is what is seen (மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும்). 331 faults the understanding that takes the unlasting for lasting. 349 explains why the error in 331 matters: for one still attached, impermanence is the standing condition, and Parimelazhagar on 331 likewise ties the error to attachment and rebirth.

332 likens the coming of great wealth to a crowd gathering at a dance hall and its going to that crowd dispersing. 592 says possession of goods does not stay and slips away (பொருளுடைமை நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்), while possession of inner drive is real possession. The impermanence of wealth taught to the renouncer is restated in the Book of Wealth, where it becomes a reason to value energy and not a reason to withdraw.

332 says great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) arrives and leaves like a theatre crowd, with no exception stated. 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude does not decay and is a support to his descendants (சிதைவின்றி எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). If 332 is read as a claim about all wealth, 112's durable wealth contradicts it; the conflict eases if 332 is taken, with Parimelazhagar, as wealth that stays only while its cause in good deeds lasts.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however it is guarded, and what is one's own will not go even if thrown out (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). 332 says wealth comes and goes like a crowd at a show. 376 puts a cause behind 332's picture: coming and going follow one's allotted portion; Parimelazhagar reads 332 the same way, the crowd coming for the dance and leaving when it ends.

333 says wealth by nature does not stay, so on getting it one should at once do what stays (அது பெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). 226 says removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where one who has got wealth should deposit it (பெற்றான் பொருள்வைப்புழி). 226 names a concrete instance of the lasting thing 333 leaves open; Parimelazhagar glosses 333's lasting things as worship and giving done without looking for return.

437 says the wealth of the miser who does not do with it what should be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது) perishes without anything surviving. 333 says wealth does not stay and should be turned at once into what does. The Book of Wealth gives the same instruction negatively: unused wealth is simply lost.

334 says what shows itself as a 'day' is a blade sawing through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. 38 says doing good so that no day falls wasted (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) becomes a stone that blocks the road of one's days (வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as blocking further embodied life. Both count life in days; 38 says how the days that 334 shows being cut away can be used so that the counting stops.

334 presents each day as a blade cutting life, with no one exempted. 326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது) of one who lives by not killing. Read literally, 326 exempts the non-killer from the daily loss of life that 334 treats as universal; the conflict depends on taking 326 as a promise about lifespan and not as praise of the vow.

335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 36 says do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது), for it is the undying companion when one dies (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). Both forbid postponing virtue to the deathbed; 335 gives the physical reason, that at that hour one cannot even speak.

342 says if you want what renunciation brings, renounce while there is still something (உண்டாகத் துறக்க), which Parimelazhagar takes as 'while there is time'. 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle. On that reading the next chapter applies the same urgency to renouncing that 335 applies to good deeds.

336 says this world has the 'greatness' that one who was here yesterday is not here today (நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை). 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except high renown (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில்). 233 agrees with 336 about everything else and names one exception; the renouncer's chapter offers none.

336 says a person who was yesterday is not today (இன்றில்லை). 235 speaks of a death that is really existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு), possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains as the body of fame surviving. The two verses use the same pair, உள and இல், in opposite directions: 336 for the plain fact of death and 235 for the rare death that leaves something that is.

no_link_reason: Its claim (people unsure of living one more moment entertain countless thoughts) is restated only by neighbouring verses of its own chapter; links to the verses on craving or on planning would rest on Parimelazhagar's gloss of the 'thoughts', not on the Tamil.

links.note: 338 says the friendship between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell or nest (குடம்பை) behind. In 1122 the lover says the bond between him and the girl is whatever the bond between body and life is (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்ன மற்றன்ன ... நட்பு). The same phrase is used with opposite force: the lover uses it for closeness, and 338 has already said that this bond ends in desertion; Parimelazhagar notes that 1122 is spoken in fear of parting.

73 reports that the bond of life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way of being joined with love. 338 calls the same bond a நட்பு that ends as a bird leaves its shell. 73 gives the union a purpose, a life lived in love; 338 gives its term. Read together, the body is a temporary partner that exists for something.

338 pictures the body as a குடம்பை, shell or nest, that the bird leaves empty; 340 pictures it as a lodging (துச்சில்) where life stays as a tenant without a home of its own (புக்கில்). Both make the body a dwelling and life its occupant. 338 shows the departure, and 340 asks why there has to be one; Manakkudavar takes the permanent home to be liberation.

339 says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking from sleep (உறங்குவது போலுஞ் சாக்காடு). 926 says those asleep are no different from the dead (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்), in order to say drinkers are always eating poison. The same equation of sleep and death runs both ways: 339 makes death as ordinary as sleep, 926 makes sleep, and so stupor, as bad as death; Parimelazhagar says the likeness in 926 is the absence of awareness.

339 presents death and birth as alternating like sleep and waking, which both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read as a cycle that keeps turning. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). 356 limits 339: the waking that follows each death is the rule only for those who have not seen the real.

340 asks whether the life that has stayed as a lodger in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has not found a permanent home. 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess (உடம்பும் மிகை). 340 says the body is not life's own house; the chapter on renunciation draws the conclusion, that the seeker treats the body itself as one possession too many.
